{{Short description|Nonparametric two-sample test methods}}
'''Ball Divergence (BD)''' is a nonparametric two‐sample statistic that quantifies the discrepancy between two probability measures <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> on a metric space {{nowrap|<math>(V,\rho)</math>.}}<ref name="Pan. BD 2002">{{Cite journal |last1=Pan |first1=Wenliang |last2=Tian |first2=Yuan |last3=Wang |first3=Xueqin |last4=Zhang |first4=Heping |date=2018-06-01 |title=Ball Divergence: Nonparametric two sample test |journal=The Annals of Statistics |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=1109–1137 |doi=10.1214/17-AOS1579 |pmid=30344356 |pmc=6192286 |issn=0090-5364}}</ref> It is defined by integrating the squared difference of the measures over all closed balls in <math>V</math>. Let <math>\overline B(u,r) = \{w\in V\mid \rho(u,w)\le r\}</math> be the closed ball of radius <math>r\ge0</math> centered at {{nowrap|<math>u\in V</math>.}} Equivalently, one may set <math>r = \rho(u,v)</math> and write {{nowrap|<math>\overline B\bigl(u,\rho(u,v)\bigr)</math>.}} The Ball divergence is then defined by
<math display="block">
BD(\mu,\nu)=
\iint_{V\times V}
\bigl[\mu(\overline B(u,\rho(u,v))) - \nu(\overline B(u,\rho(u,v)))\bigr]^{2}
\; \bigl[\mu(du)\,\mu(dv) + \nu(du)\,\nu(dv)\bigr].
</math>
This measure can be seen as an integral of the [[Harald Cramér]]'s distance over all possible pairs of points. By summing squared differences of <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> over balls of all scales, BD captures both global and local discrepancies between distributions, yielding a robust, scale-sensitive comparison. Moreover, since BD is defined as the integral of a squared measure difference, it is always non-negative, and <math>BD(\mu,\nu)=0</math> if and only if <math>\mu=\nu</math>.

==Testing for equal distributions==

Next, we will try to give a sample version of Ball Divergence. For convenience, we can decompose the Ball Divergence into two parts:
<math display="block">
A=\iint_{V \times V}[\mu-\nu]^2(\bar{B}(u, \rho(u, v))) \mu(d u) \mu(d v),
</math>
and
<math display="block">
C=\iint_{V \times V}[\mu-\nu]^2(\bar{B}(u, \rho(u, v))) \nu(d u) \nu(d v) .
</math>
Thus <math>
BD(\mu, \nu)=A+C .
</math>

Let <math> \delta(x, y, z)=I(z \in \bar{B}(x, \rho(x, y))) </math> denote whether point <math> z </math> locates in the ball <math> \bar{B}(x, \rho(x, y)) </math>. Given two independent samples <math> \{ X_1,\ldots, X_n \} </math> form <math> \mu </math> and <math> \{ Y_1,\ldots, Y_m \} </math> form <math> \nu </math>

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
A_{i j}^X &= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{u=1}^n \delta{\left(X_i, X_j, X_u\right)}, & A_{i j}^Y &= \frac{1}{m} \sum_{v=1}^m \delta{\left(X_i, X_j, Y_v\right)}, \\
C_{k l}^X &= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{u=1}^n \delta{\left(Y_k, Y_l, X_u\right)}, & C_{i j}^Y &= \frac{1}{m} \sum_{v=1}^m \delta{\left(Y_k, Y_l, Y_v\right)},
\end{align}
</math>
where <math> A_{i j}^X </math> means the proportion of samples from the probability measure <math> \mu </math> located in the ball <math> \bar{B}\left(X_i, \rho\left(X_i, X_j\right)\right) </math> and <math> A_{i j}^Y </math> means the proportion of samples from the probability measure <math> \nu </math> located in the ball <math> \bar{B}\left(X_i, \rho\left(X_i, X_j\right)\right) </math>. Meanwhile, <math> C_{i j}^X </math> and <math> C_{i j}^Y </math> means the proportion of samples from the probability measure <math> \mu </math> and <math> \nu </math> located in the ball <math> \bar{B}\left(Y_i, \rho\left(Y_i, Y_j\right)\right) </math>. The sample versions of <math> A </math> and <math> C </math> are as follows

<math display="block">
A_{n, m}=\frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i, j=1}^n\left(A_{i j}^X-A_{i j}^Y\right)^2, \qquad C_{n, m}=\frac{1}{m^2} \sum_{k, l=1}^m\left(C_{k l}^X-C_{k l}^Y\right)^2.
</math>

Finally, we can give the sample ball divergence

<math display="block">BD_{n, m} = A_{n, m}+C_{n, m}.</math>

It can be proved that <math>BD_{n,m}</math> is a [[consistent estimator]] of BD. Moreover, if <math display="inline">\tfrac{n}{n+m}\to\tau</math> for some <math>\tau\in[0,1]</math>, then under the null hypothesis <math>BD_{n,m}</math> converges in distribution to a mixture of chi-squared distributions, whereas under the [[alternative hypothesis]] it converges to a [[normal distribution]].

==Properties==

# The square root of Ball Divergence is a symmetric divergence but not a metric, because it does not satisfy the [[triangle inequality]].
# It can be shown that Ball divergence, [[energy distance test]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Székely |first1=Gábor J. |last2=Rizzo |first2=Maria L. |date=August 2013 |title=Energy statistics: A class of statistics based on distances |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.jspi.2013.03.018 |journal=Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference |volume=143 |issue=8 |pages=1249–1272 |doi=10.1016/j.jspi.2013.03.018 |issn=0378-3758|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and MMD<ref>{{Citation |last1=Gretton |first1=Arthur |chapter=A Kernel Method for the Two-Sample-Problem |date=2007-09-07 |title=Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 19 |pages=513–520 |chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.7551/mitpress/7503.003.0069 |access-date=2024-06-28 |publisher=The MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-25691-9 |last2=Borgwardt |first2=Karsten M. |last3=Rasch |first3=Malte |last4=Schölkopf |first4=Bernhard |last5=Smola |first5=Alexander J.|doi=10.7551/mitpress/7503.003.0069 |hdl=1885/37327 |hdl-access=free |chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> are unified within the variogram framework; for details see Remark 2.4 in.<ref name="Pan. BD 2002"/>

==Homogeneity Test==
Ball divergence admits a straightforward extension to the K-sample setting. Suppose <math>\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K</math> are <math>K (\ge2)</math> probability measures on a Banach space <math>(V,\|\cdot\|)</math>. Define the K-sample BD by

<math display="block">
D(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_K)
=\sum_{1\le k<l\le K}
\iint_{V\times V}
\bigl[\mu_k\bigl(\overline B(u,\rho(u,v))\bigr)
-\mu_l\bigl(\overline B(u,\rho(u,v))\bigr)\bigr]^{2}
\;\bigl[\mu_k(du)\,\mu_k(dv)+\mu_l(du)\,\mu_l(dv)\bigr].
</math>

It then follows from Theorems 1 and 2 that <math>D(\mu_1,\dots,\mu_K)=0</math> if and only if <math>\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_K.</math>

By employing closed balls to define a metric distribution function, one obtains an alternative homogeneity measure.<ref>Wang, X., Zhu, J., Pan, W., Zhu, J., & Zhang, H. (2023). Nonparametric Statistical Inference via Metric Distribution Function in Metric Spaces. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 119(548), 2772–2784. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.2023.2277417</ref>

Given a probability measure <math>\tilde\mu</math> on a metric space <math>(V,\rho)</math>, its '''metric distribution function''' is defined by

<math display="block">
F^{M}_{\tilde\mu}(u,v)
=\tilde\mu\bigl(\overline B(u,\rho(u,v))\bigr)=\mathbb E\bigl[\delta(u,v,X)\bigr],
\quad u,v\in V,
</math>

where <math>\overline B(u,r) = \{w\in V:d(u,w)\le r\}</math> is the closed ball of radius <math>r\ge0</math> centered at <math>u</math>, and <math>\delta(u,v,X)
=\prod_{k=1}^K\mathbf 1\{X^{(k)}\in \overline B_k(u_k,\rho_k(u_k,v_k))\}.</math>

If <math>(X_1,\dots,X_N)</math> are i.i.d. draws from <math>(\tilde\mu)</math>, the empirical version is

<math display="block">
F^{M}_{\tilde\mu,N}(u,v)
=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta(u,v,X_i).
</math>

Based on these, the '''homogeneity measure''' based on MDF, also called metric Cramér-von Mises (MCVM) is
<math display="block">
\mathrm{MCVM}\bigl(\mu_{k}\parallel\mu\bigr)
=\int_{V\times V}
p_{k}^{2}\,w(u,v)\,
\bigl[F^{M}_{\mu_{k}}(u,v)
- F^{M}_{\mu}(u,v)\bigr]^{2}
\,d\mu_{k}(u)\,d\mu_{k}(v),
</math>

where <math display="inline">\mu=\sum_{k=1}^{K} p_{k}\,\mu_{k}</math> be their mixture with weights <math>p_{1},\dots,p_{K}</math>, and <math display="inline">w(u,v)=\exp\left(-\tfrac{d(u,v)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)</math>.
The overall MCVM is then

<math display="block">
\mathrm{MCVM}(\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{K})
=\sum_{k=1}^{K}p_{k}^{2}\,\mathrm{MCVM}\bigl(\mu_{k}\parallel\mu\bigr).
</math>

The empirical MCVM is given by

<math display="block">
\widehat{\mathrm{MCVM}}\bigl(\mu_{k}\parallel\mu\bigr)
=\frac{1}{n_{k}^{2}}
\sum_{X^{(k)}_{i},X^{(k)}_{j}\in\mathcal X_{k}}
w\bigl(X^{(k)}_{i},X^{(k)}_{j}\bigr)\,
\left[
F^{M}_{\mu_{k},n_{k}}\bigl(X^{(k)}_{i},X^{(k)}_{j}\bigr)
- F^{M}_{\mu,n}\bigl(X^{(k)}_{i},X^{(k)}_{j}\bigr)
\right]^2.
</math>

where <math>\mathcal X_{k}=\{X^{(k)}_{1},\dots,X^{(k)}_{n_{k}}\}</math> be an i.i.d. sample from <math>\mu_{k}</math>, and <math>\hat p_{k}=\frac{n_{k}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}n_{\ell}}.</math>
A practical choice for <math>\sigma^{2}</math> is the median of the squared distances
<math display="block">\left\{d(X,X')^{2}:X,X'\in\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}\mathcal X_{k}\right\}.</math>
